Ten questions, one graph. articles.title: The graph companies: many of the most valuable companies in the world are graphs, of links, people, products, payments and ontologies, and the graphs never scaled for everyone else because they were built to lock in
articles.teaser: Four of the ten most valuable companies are graph companies. Graphs never scaled for everyone else because they were built to lock in. Now they can.

figures.caption: The graph companies. Market values on 19 October 2026, with the graph at the heart of each: Alphabet, $4.17 trillion, the link graph and the Knowledge Graph; Microsoft, $3.96 trillion, which owns LinkedIn's economic graph; Amazon, $2.84 trillion, the product graph and the logistics network; Meta, $1.79 trillion, the social graph; Visa, $755 billion, and Mastercard, $538 billion, payment networks; Palantir, $469 billion, an ontology of the organisation. Four of the ten most valuable companies in the world are on the list.

The answer becomes obvious. On the left, a graph with every node and edge: people, places, events, evidence, and no answer in sight. In the middle, the irrelevant nodes removed, the relevant connections kept. On the right, what is left: a short path from the question to the answer, which now looks obvious. The same move works for a supply chain, a contract, a regulation, or a search result.

Why graphs never scaled, and how they can now. Before: building a graph took a lot of technology; whoever built it used it to lock in the customer and keep competitors out; there was no movement to share schemas or the code; so each graph stayed inside one company, and the advantage stayed with the few. Now: fractal semantic graphs, where each part keeps its own vocabulary and nobody has to share a schema; open source and open schemas; agents that build and maintain the graph; so graphs can be built by anyone, for any domain.

articles.title: Governs, enforces, attests: what an Agent Behaviour Policy does, the three levels at which its rules are kept, and why an attestation layer on top is the piece a third party needs
articles.teaser: An ABP governs and names the enforcer at three levels: prompt, hooks, or a third-party system. An attestation layer signs it so a third party can verify.

figures.caption: Four layers of the same stack. At the top, the mandate: an Agent Behaviour Policy per role, saying what the role is granted, what it is for, the rules, and how each rule is kept. Below it, enforcement at three levels: the prompt, hooks in the harness, and a third-party system that blocks, such as Ruflo's policy engine in enforce mode. Below that, the record: Ruflo's decision receipt for every action, and an sgit vault keeping memory and receipts encrypted and versioned. At the bottom, attestation: what was assured, signed, so that someone outside can verify it. The first three exist in ruv.sgit; the fourth is the attestation layer.

Three levels of enforcement for one rule of an Agent Behaviour Policy. Level 1, the prompt: the rule is in the agent's instructions; it sees everything and enforces nothing; the agent can ignore it; the evidence is the agent's own account. Level 2, hooks: small deterministic programs the harness runs before and after each action; they can block, but they sit on the agent's machine and are often editable by its account; the evidence is the hook's log. Level 3, a third-party system: a policy engine, gateway or service that does the blocking, out of the agent's reach; the evidence is that system's decision record. The recommended level for any rule that matters is the third.

The same question, from a customer, an auditor or an insurer: was this agent working under that policy, and was each rule kept? Without an attestation layer: the operator sends the policy, the logs and the receipts; the third party cannot tell which version was in force, whether the receipts were edited, or which rules were only in the prompt; they take the operator's word. With an attestation layer: what was assured is signed, the policy version, the level of each rule, the receipts and the record's hash; the third party verifies the signature and reads what was and was not enforced; trust moves from the operator's word to a check.

One action through the stack. The agent proposes a tool call. A hook checks it on the machine, as an early warning. The third-party policy engine decides allow or deny, in enforce mode, and writes a decision receipt. The receipt and the agent's memory go into the sgit vault, encrypted and versioned. The attestation layer signs what was assured: the policy version, each rule's level, the receipts, the record's hash. A customer, auditor or insurer verifies the signature without access to the operator's systems.

graph.teaser: An ABP governs and names the enforcer at three levels: prompt, hooks, or a third-party system. An attestation layer signs it so a third party can verify.

articles.title: A directory of people and their keys: pki.sgit.ai for the people I work with, verified by me first, then by each other, and a link that only counts when it goes both ways
articles.teaser: pki.sgit.ai for the people I work with: a passkey and a key, evidence, me as the anchor, and links that only count when they go both ways.

figures.caption: From a passkey to a message. A person registers a passkey on pki.sgit.ai, which opens their vault; makes or imports a key pair, with the private keys kept in the vault; publishes the public half; adds evidence (a website, GitHub, a DNS record); is verified by Dinis, who signs it, and confirms that from their side; and links with others, each link counting only when both confirm. Then anyone in the register can be sent a secret as a QR code that opens in their browser and is read with their vault.

Two ways, or not at all. On the left, 2019: anyone could append a signature to anyone's key, and nothing could be deleted, so keys were flooded until they broke. On the right, the rule here: each person writes only to their own record. A vouches for B in A's record; B confirms in B's record; the link exists only when both do. A vouch that nobody confirms stays a claim in the voucher's own record, and each record has a size limit.

articles.teaser: Cloudflare's developer platform as the smallest free blocks a non-specialist can use, and an sgit vault on it: no code read-only, 83 lines read-write.

figures.caption: Cloudflare's developer platform as blocks, grouped by job. Put something on the web: static assets, free and unlimited; Workers, 100,000 requests a day; DNS and domains at cost. Keep data: R2 with 10 GB and zero egress, D1, KV, Durable Objects. Think with models it hosts: Workers AI with 10,000 neurons a day on Cloudflare's own GPUs, AI Gateway, Vectorize and AI Search. Run jobs: cron, queues and workflows, Browser Run, and Containers on the paid plan. Talk and guard: inbound email routing, email sending on the paid plan, Access free to 50 users, Turnstile and Tunnel.
medium

articles.teaser: RiskMandate and the Agent Behaviour Policy in plain words: what it does, why it is not real time, which agents it covers, and how it gets into the room.

figures.caption: One agent, three sets. The grant is everything the agent can actually reach through its credentials and connectors; the mandate is what the organisation authorised it to do; the delta is the difference, the authority nobody accepted. Each capability in the grant carries a barrier: nothing in the way, a rule in prose, a setting the agent's own account can change, or a boundary enforced above it. Only the last bounds anything.

Five ways into the room, each a question someone already has to answer: a contract, where legal and procurement ask what the vendor's agent will do with the data; a security questionnaire, where a customer asks which agents touch their data; an insurance renewal, where the question is whether AI is excluded from cover; the board's risk appetite, where the question is who can pull the plug; and twenty minutes, where anyone running an assistant asks what it can actually do.

articles.title: Case law for agents: principles from the top, precedent from the cases, and how a decision earns its way into code
articles.teaser: Nobody predicts every case. Borrow the shape of English case law: escalate what the policy does not settle, record it, follow it, then compile it.

figures.caption: How a decision earns its way into code. A case arrives at a branch point. If a rule settles it, or a recorded precedent with the same material facts matches, it is resolved and recorded. If not, or if the facts differ in a way that matters, it is distinguished and escalated to a person with the context to decide. The decision is recorded with its reasons and becomes a precedent that the next matching case follows. A precedent that holds case after case is written into the policy, then compiled into deterministic, tested code.

graph.teaser: Nobody predicts every case. Borrow the shape of English case law: escalate what the policy does not settle, record it, follow it, then compile it.
graph.core_idea: Decision policies handle unpredicted cases the way common law does: principles from the top, escalation to a person for cases no rule or precedent settles, recorded decisions that bind the next matching case, distinguishing as the escalation trigger, and precedents that keep holding written into policy and then compiled into code.

articles.title: When is the vault actually used? In Mondweep Chakravorty's SGit × Ruflo run, the encrypted vault is written or read in three steps of twelve, on one machine, inside the adapter, and why that is the honest shape of a recovery copy
articles.teaser: In the SGit × Ruflo run the vault is written or read in three steps of twelve, on one machine, inside the adapter: the right shape for a recovery copy.

figures.caption: Who does what, step by step: the vault is written or read in steps 5, 8 and 11, protected in step 6 and survives step 7; Ruflo's own command line touches memory in steps 3, 9 and 10, where the ABP is not on the path. From the architecture addendum to the analysis of Mondweep Chakravorty's video.

The component map: the test script calls Ruflo's command line in steps 3, 9 and 10 and the ABP adapter's tools in steps 4, 5, 6, 8 and 11; the ABP rows are compiled to Ruflo rules and checked by a pinned copy of Ruflo's evaluator in enforce mode, which leads to the SGit library, which writes the vault and its keys on the machine's disk. Ruflo's hive-mind, its running policy state and a remote vault server were not used. Blue is Ruflo, amber the ABP adapter, green SGit and the vault, grey plain files.

Step 5: the checkpoint tool passes the policy gate; a SQLite backup takes a consistent copy of memory.db; fingerprints of the database, the ABP and the policy are taken; the SGit library encrypts on the machine and writes ciphertext only to the checkpoint store, with keys kept apart.

Step 8: a new MCP server process restores the checkpoint; the policy gate allows it; the SGit library reads ciphertext from the vault and keys from the private folder, decrypts and verifies, and writes memory.sqlite into the fresh-runner workspace, with the same SHA-256 as in step 5.

Step 11: one object in the vault is altered; the restore tool passes the policy gate; the adapter compares the digest of the stored ciphertext with the one recorded in step 5, finds a mismatch, and a ValueError means the tampered workspace is never created; SGit is never asked to decrypt.
Where the video's vault lives: on one machine, the adapter and SGit library, the checkpoint store, the private key folder and the workspaces; a vault server was not used.

articles.title: The fork next door: why open source protects founders, customers and investors from each other, why forks only take hold when someone stops executing, and why a maturing company should give its explorers a way out
articles.teaser: Founders, customers and investors are each protected from the others because anyone can fork; forks take hold only after a breakdown.

figures.caption: Three corners, one exit each: the open code sits in the middle, and each corner can take it and carry on. The founders can leave if no broad non-compete stops them; the investors can fund a team next door if they can pay for it; the customers can move if their data leaves with them, cheaply. Illustrative.

Six forks: what broke, the year each fork began, and what happened next. MariaDB stayed a hedge while MySQL kept shipping; io.js merged back once a foundation fixed the governance; LibreOffice, Nextcloud, OpenTofu and Valkey took hold after a new owner, a change of direction or a licence change.

Commits a year to the trunk branch of mysql/mysql-server: about 8,900 in 2019 and about 2,800 in 2025, a fall of roughly two thirds. 2026 runs to 28 September. Measured by this site from a clone of the repository.

Forking is a last resort and the famous forks that took hold followed a breakdown; where the original kept executing, the fork stayed a hedge. A risky practice can be unrelated to success across everyone and still look like its cause among survivors. Illustrative.

Who is the commodity: in music, the songs, the producers, the venues and radio stay scarce while the performer is moved towards commodity; in venture, the investor's network stays scarce while the founder is moved the same way. A sketch of the argument, not a measured map.

Control moves with performance: when a company performs poorly, investors take full control; as it improves, the founder gains control; when it performs very well, investors keep their cash-flow rights but give up most control. A schematic of Kaplan and Strömberg's finding, not their data.

articles.title: Sell, don't issue: a funding model for founders who have already won, where the investor buys the founder's shares, the founder lends the company what it needs, and open source keeps everyone honest
articles.teaser: For founders who have already won: the investor buys the founder's shares, the founder lends the company what it needs, and open source keeps everyone honest.

figures.caption: The two-part model: the investor buys the founder's ordinary shares and pays the founder; the founder lends part of the proceeds to the company as a subordinated loan; the company gets cash without new shares; and the investor's protection is the open-source fork, not a board seat.

The same £2 million, two ways, for a UK company worth £10 million: the founder keeps 80% either way; a standard round gives the investor new preferred shares, rights and control, and puts £2 million into the company; selling and lending gives the investor ordinary shares and the fork as protection, and leaves the founder about £1.58 million after tax, to lend back as much as the company needs; and bought shares carry no EIS relief.

articles.title: Research, delivered as a vault: what companies that sell research could do with fractal graphs, behaviour policies for AI-enabled products, and evaluations run by a governed agent hive

figures.caption: The example vault's cover: a synthetic research firm's assessment of a synthetic accounts payable product with and without its AI agent; insurability B before, D after, B again with four conditions; reach from 4 to 6 systems; three rules that rest on the model behaving.

The example vault's fractal graph: the question opens into the vendor, the product, the AI agent and the buyer's systems, then capabilities, the rules that govern them, findings, evidence and the agent worker that produced each piece of evidence.

The same research delivered two ways: a report gives one document for every reader, a rating as a field, evidence described, a category and a row, a reissue next year, a document that is read and filed, an attachment; a vault gives a briefing per reader, a judgement over facts anyone can check, the evidence attached, a fractal graph, a refresh as a new commit with a diff, a lane to write back, and access by key.

The example's two behaviour policies: four rules before the AI agent, all held by boundaries and settings; eight after, three of them held only by hope that the model follows its instructions, including the one on supplier bank details.

Licence to operate and insurability in the example: B before the AI agent, D after, B with four conditions the vendor can meet; the grade is the research firm's judgement over facts that are all in the vault.

The loop a research firm could sell: a live evaluation, the vault, a briefing per reader, the client writing back, and a refresh when the vendor ships a change, which starts the next run; each step a line on the invoice. Proposed.

articles.title: sgit is a standard, not a server: everything in a vault is one hash away, any storage can serve it, and the server is the least interesting part
articles.teaser: Git won as a standard, not a server. sgit is one too: every name computed from the key, a file four GETs away, any storage can serve it.

figures.caption: Everything in a vault is one hash away: the vault key gives the read key, the read key gives the ref's name by an HMAC, and the ref, the commit, the trees on the path and the blob are plain GETs; reads come from any host that answers a GET, writes need a compare-and-swap, and caching is by name, not by header.

Deploying sgit is choosing where the objects live: a folder; a laptop running the hosted image; your own server; a static host such as GitHub Pages; or the hosted service, a Lambda in front of S3 behind CloudFront; from closer and faster to further and shared.

graph.teaser: Git won as a standard, not a server. sgit is one too: every name computed from the key, a file four GETs away, any storage can serve it.
graph.core_idea: Like git, sgit is a format rather than a product: encrypted blobs, trees, commits and refs laid out by a convention, immutable objects named by the hash of their ciphertext and marked -imm-, every name derived from the key so a file is four GETs from any host, writes one batch and a compare-and-swap, two implementations that agree; deployment is choosing where the objects live and speed is how close they are; a cache layer computed by the writer replaces server-side derived data; and the design is what remains when the server cannot read.

articles.title: The value of constraints: what client-side encryption and open source actually gave us, which is not what you would think
articles.teaser: sgit's encryption and open source matter less as features than as constraints: they remove the temptations that lead to server code, lock-in and bad decisions.

figures.caption: Two constraints and what they take away: client-side encryption forbids the server from reading the data and removes the temptation to process there; open source, all of it, forbids private code and removes lock-in, the evaluation edition and building every customer's integration.

Encryption on the client moves the problem from the data to the keys: a server that can read has to protect all the data, runs code next to it, and puts the sovereignty line where the data is; a server that holds ciphertext needs the keys protected, runs no code next to the data, and puts the line at whoever holds the keys.

graph.teaser: sgit's encryption and open source matter less as features than as constraints: they remove the temptations that lead to server code, lock-in and bad decisions.

articles.title: Scion and sgit: Anthropic rebuilt source control for agents inside one company, and an open-source encrypted version already does much of the same thing outside it
articles.teaser: Anthropic's Scion replaced Git for agents inside one company; sgit, open source and encrypted, shares its core ideas, measured on a 35,000-object vault.

figures.caption: Two answers to agents at scale: Scion's always-online clients, three cache tiers and a server that does history, blame, merges and commits; and sgit's clients that encrypt, merge and read history, a dumb server that stores encrypted objects in batches of 50, and reads that any static host can serve, from objects any cache can keep.

Scion, sgit and Git side by side: who does the work, whether the server holds plaintext, how a folder is protected, object ids, packing, partial copies, reads without the server, writes, merge, history, implementations, deployment, proven scale and availability.

The measurements now: the 83-file vault this article first measured, 59 seconds with sgit 0.22.0 and about 11 with the fix, 4 seconds for one folder, 1.6 from a plain static host; and the 35,000-object vault the newsroom's agents share, 210 seconds in full, 57 with one commit of history, 13 for one folder with one commit.

The Vault tab in the pane, 400 pixels wide, in Newsprint, with two devices ticked in Across your devices. The bar under the table offers to merge them into one of the two, under a name that can be changed, and says that nothing is deleted. The total row is the account recomputed from the records.

How the viewer is linked. Left, a reader vault: its records under activity/, and four small files the next Update writes. Right, the newsroom's viewer in vault lkypj6zq, with its code. articles.title: Cedar and the policy vault: a debrief on the policy language agents are adopting, where our behaviour policies and sgit vaults meet it, and a brief for the MVP
articles.teaser: Cedar is mature and adopted; it lacks the why, the version in force and the evidence. A vault carries all three, and the demo shows it working.

figures.caption: Cedar policies in an sgit vault, from the rule to the evidence: a gate that validates every version against the schema and its tests, tags signed by the releasing clone, enforcement points that clone with the read key only, and an append lane that keeps a sealed record of every decision. What ran in the demo for this article is solid; the gateway and the sync into managed stores are proposed.

Our behaviour-policy terms, Cedar's, and where each one lives in the vault. Most map directly: the grant is permit, the barrier is forbid, the footprint is the entities. Two have no Cedar construct, the mandate and the version in force, and those are what the vault adds.

Amazon Verified Permissions as its documentation describes it, a plain repository, and the vault from the demo. The managed store validates strictly and is protected by IAM, but its API has no history or export, and deleting it is permanent. A repository has history but no keys. The vault has both, and puts the evidence next to the rules.

graph.teaser: Cedar is mature and adopted; it lacks the why, the version in force and the evidence. A vault carries all three, and the demo shows it working.

articles.title: The eyeballs get cheap: why open source is about to become the most secure software we have, and why secure, sovereign and paid-for meet at the least code in production
articles.teaser: Cheap, deep AI security review gives open source the eyeballs it never had; with sovereignty and paid maintenance, all point at the least code in production.

figures.caption: Open source against proprietary: the balance that just moved. Open source had the source in view and paid for few reviews; proprietary had the budget and the cover of being hidden. Cheap, deep, model-driven security review changes one side of that balance far more than the other.

One project, one year of machine eyeballs: curl, from its maintainer's own posts. A bug bounty that found 87 vulnerabilities; a year of reports that were mostly noise; a first wave of AI-assisted reports that triggered hundreds of fixes; the end of the bounty; a frontier scan that found one bug; and, in October, deeper tools finding more.

Three forces meeting at the least code in production: open source becoming very secure, open source becoming required for sovereignty, and open source with commercial models that pay for maintenance. Where they meet is the customer running exactly the code they need, maintained by the people who know it best.

articles.teaser: A skill behaviour policy compares what a skill says, what it can do and what it is given, then generates the control; measured on 899 skills.

899 skills from three public sources, every file read as text and nothing run: what they can reach, and what their descriptions leave out. 812 can reach something beyond their own scripts, 782 of them through one third-party tool server; 39 have a feature their description does not mention; none was obfuscated, and none sets allowed-tools.

articles.title: Are hooks the sweet spot? Moving an agent's rules from hope into hooks, rule by rule, until enforcement moves off the machine
articles.teaser: One agent's eleven rules, moved from the prompt into hooks and tested: four fully, two mostly, three partly, two not at all, and a gap in the leak scan.

Moved into hooks and tested on fixed inputs in a throwaway repository: four fully, two mostly, three partly, two not at all.

Where a rule can be kept. From the prompt, which sees everything and enforces nothing, through agent hooks and the tools' own hooks, to the sandbox, a gateway off the machine, and the service itself. Each layer down is harder for the agent to change and sees less of what the agent meant to do.

Where a hook sits: beside the agent, on the same machine, with the user's permissions. articles.title: The minimum code below: container security from the top down, from the user story to the immutable line, measured on one real tool
articles.teaser: Container security from the top down: at every layer, keep only the code the layer above needs. Measured on one real tool, with its limits.

figures.caption: Top down, one question at every layer: what is the minimum code below this that the layer above needs? From a user story, through the workflow, modules and functions, to the dependencies, the language runtime and the operating system. Projected from the top, derived from the code; derived and not projected is code nobody asked for.

One use case, measured. sgit 0.21.0 and its dependencies, run under coverage for a CI-style use case, then run again from a tree holding only the files that ran: 1,500 files down to 428, Python source from 4.72 MB to 1.98 MB, compiled code unchanged at 14.78 MB. Inside the kept files 38% of the statements ran; commands outside the use case failed; coverage missed a compiled module the tests caught.

Three ways to get to less code. Bottom up and hardened, as Chainguard does; runtime minimisation, as SlimToolkit and RapidFort do; and top down by use case, proposed here, which starts from what the application is for and ties every remaining line to a reason.

graph.teaser: Container security from the top down: at every layer, keep only the code the layer above needs. Measured on one real tool, with its limits.
graph.core_idea: Bottom-up hardening still leaves code the application never runs, so security should also come from the top: starting from the use case, ask at every layer for the minimum code below and remove the rest; measured on sgit, a use case ran from 428 of 1,500 files while compiled code and coverage blind spots set the limits, and a graph traced from story to build makes the result certifiable.

articles.title: sgit in a CI pipeline: encrypted, versioned data in and out of GitHub Actions, between its jobs, through write-only lanes, and a key for every job
articles.teaser: Encrypted, versioned vaults as the way data gets into, out of and between CI jobs, with a key per job and a sidecar when there is no server.

figures.caption: A pipeline whose stages talk through a vault. Each job clones only the folders it needs, with only the key it needs: build writes with the vault key, test shards append to write-only inboxes, the summary reads the lane, release and deploy read with the read key and their own key pairs, and anyone outside GitHub can clone the results with a read key. What leaves a runner is ciphertext.

Which job holds which key. Build and the summary hold the vault key, release, deploy and outside readers the read key, each test shard one append token, the summary the lane's enum key, and the jobs that sign or decrypt their own key pair. The server access token opens a private server's door for everyone; it is not a vault permission.

No hosted server. The vault server runs as a container inside the job with its storage in a folder; the folder holds only ciphertext, so it can be saved to the Actions cache, an artifact, a release asset or a git branch, and the next run restores it and clones with its full history. Reading needs no server at all; pushing needs the server's API, which the sidecar provides.

graph.teaser: Encrypted, versioned vaults as the way data gets into, out of and between CI jobs, with a key per job and a sidecar when there is no server.
graph.core_idea: A CI pipeline needs a versioned, encrypted record that outlives its runs and can be read outside GitHub, and sgit vaults provide it: jobs push and clone only their folders with --path, keys rather than scopes set what each job may do, append lanes collect shard results write-only, per-job key pairs make wiring mistakes fail loudly, and a sidecar server with a cached ciphertext folder removes the need for a hosted server.

articles.teaser: A new homepage edition every morning, each a signed commit in a vault, served from plain files: every past homepage one commit id away.

figures.caption: The homepage as a vault: a morning job writes an edition and tags it, the encrypted objects go to plain static hosting, a small shell on GitHub Pages carries the read key and a snapshot for search engines, and the browser reads the edition. A stats lane and a daily run of synthetic users feed the next morning's edition. Dashed boxes are proposed.

Three editions of the demo homepage vault, each a commit with a signed tag, carrying its page, the links it showed and why, both variants, its release note and a screenshot of itself. Any edition opens again from its commit id.

One page load: the shell from GitHub Pages, then four chained requests to the static host for the ref, the commit, the tree and the page, decrypted in the browser; the dynamic slots load from their own vaults; a beacon goes to the stats lane. articles.title: Attacks rewritten as mandates: 28 supply-chain incidents, the column each one was missing, and why the next maintainer is an agent
articles.teaser: 28 supply-chain attacks read as reach beyond mandate: what a hardened registry stops, what only a written mandate can, and why agents change it.

figures.caption: The ledger. Chainguard's 28 public supply-chain incidents, May 2024 to October 2026, each dot one incident, coloured by its first vector; 23 of them are from 2026. Below, every vector counted, by our reading: an install-time hook ran the payload in 17, a maintainer account or token was taken over in 16.

For each of the 28 incidents, the control that would most likely have stopped it, by our reading: on the consumer's side, what you let in; on the publisher's side, what a credential was for. A consumer-side control appears in 26, a publisher-side mandate in 16, both in 14. And one case where the consumer was a model.
One pipeline, three records: what an agent consumes, what it was allowed to do, and what it produced and remembers. The first has products; the second and third are what RiskMandate and sgit work on.

graph.teaser: 28 supply-chain attacks read as reach beyond mandate: what a hardened registry stops, what only a written mandate can, and why agents change it.
graph.core_idea: Every incident in a public ledger of 28 supply-chain attacks is a credential, tag or build step that could do more than it was meant to, so consumer-side controls a registry sells would likely have held in 26 and publisher-side mandates in 16; as agents become the maintainers that hold tokens and add dependencies, the pipeline needs three records, trusted inputs, a written mandate and provable outputs with memory, and small open source projects need a path onto the trusted list.

articles.title: Four frameworks, one agent: iason's comparison of the OECD classification, the NIST AI RMF, Japan's guidelines and the EU AI Act, read against what runs here, with the evidence and the graphs
articles.teaser: iason's comparison of four AI risk frameworks, mapped to the behaviour policy, the footprint and the graphs that run here, with the status of each row.

figures.caption: Four frameworks, as iason's paper reads them, against what runs here. For each: the question it asks of a system, how the paper summarises it, what answers it on this site and at RiskMandate, the article or vault where that can be checked, and whether it runs, is designed or is only argued. Green runs; amber is a design; grey is an argument.

Two units. On the left, the frameworks' unit: an AI system, described by its characteristics, context and impact, given a tier, and assigned obligations, before it is deployed. On the right, the unit here: one agent in one deployment, with its reach measured, its mandate written, the gap between them typed by what stands in the way, its footprint read afterwards, and a blast radius for every row. The arrows show where each of the four frameworks attaches.

A status since, for the paper. Above the line, the dates as the paper gives them, as of November 2025: prohibitions in force from February 2025, and the rules applying in full by August 2026. Below the line, what this site's own articles recorded afterwards: the amending regulation in force from 27 July 2026, Annex III obligations from 2 December 2027, Annex I from 2 August 2028, and software a product under the EU's new liability rules from 9 December 2026. Neither row is wrong on its day.

The paper's five shared principles, each against what answers it here, the evidence, and how far it goes: runs, in green; a published design with a demo behind it, in amber. Four of the five run, on one newsroom and one agent team; risk acceptance as a record is the design.

graph.teaser: iason's comparison of four AI risk frameworks, mapped to the behaviour policy, the footprint and the graphs that run here, with the status of each row.

articles.title: A policy beside the prompt: a proposal that every agent takes a behaviour policy as an input, with enforcement and liability attached, and why aviation and payments say the vendors should want it
articles.teaser: A proposal: every agent takes a behaviour policy beside its prompt, which the vendor accepts and answers for, as aviation and payments learned to.

figures.caption: What an agent is given, today in two modes and as proposed. Over the API we write the whole system prompt, so our behaviour policy goes inside it; in the Claude apps and Claude Code the vendor's system prompt comes first and our policy goes into what we add. In both, it is text the model is asked to keep, in the same channel as every email and page it reads, and the vendor's checks are its own. Proposed: the policy as a separate, versioned input, layered over the vendor's own published policy, checked outside the model where it can be.

Fatal airliner accidents, 1995 and 2025. At 1995's rate of 2.72 per million flights, 2025's 38.7 million flights would have produced about 105 fatal accidents. There were 12. Rates from the Aviation Safety Network via Our World in Data; 2025 accidents from the Flight Safety Foundation's report of the ASN data; flights from IATA.

Where the liability for payment fraud was moved, and what followed. Each step put the loss on the party best placed to stop it, and the security followed the loss: caps for consumers, a liability shift onto whoever had not adopted chip cards, standards written by the card brands, and reimbursement of scam victims.

The proposed split. The vendor publishes its own built-in policy and accepts the deployer's; for every row it accepts, it says what enforces it and answers if it breaks. Everything the policy does not cover stays with the user, as it does today. The vendors that keep more rows as boundaries can sell that as the product.

graph.teaser: A proposal: every agent takes a behaviour policy beside its prompt, which the vendor accepts and answers for, as aviation and payments learned to.
graph.core_idea: Beside the system prompt and the prompt, every agent should take an Agent Behaviour Policy written to a published standard, which the vendor acknowledges row by row, enforces where it can, reports breaches against and eventually answers for, because agent behaviour is becoming an existential risk to the vendors through liability and trust, and aviation and payments show that safety follows when the rule, the liability and the business model point the same way.

articles.title: The policy draws the liability line: an answer to Ralf Thomas on agent accountability, and why every agent in a loop should take a behaviour policy beside its prompt
articles.teaser: An answer to Ralf Thomas: the shell game works because nothing is written down, and a behaviour policy's explicit prohibitions move the liability line.

figures.caption: The four moves of the accountability shell game, from Ralf Thomas's post, and what a written behaviour policy changes in each. Without one, every move has an easy answer; with one, the question becomes whether the product honoured what it was explicitly told.

Two directions of liability. Towards the world, the deployer answers for what its agent did, as the tribunal held in Moffatt. Between the deployer and the vendor, the written policy decides whose failure it was: inside the reach and unforbidden, the deployer's; explicitly forbidden and done anyway, the product's.

graph.teaser: An answer to Ralf Thomas: the shell game works because nothing is written down, and a behaviour policy's explicit prohibitions move the liability line.
graph.core_idea: Agent vendors can deflect accountability because nothing written stands between a customer's allow and the failure; an Agent Behaviour Policy's explicit prohibitions, still mostly hope, become the evidence that moves liability between deployer and vendor when broken, so every agent in a loop should take a policy beside its prompt and its vendor should honour and report against it.

nodes.summary: Blame the agent, blame the customer, hide behind the contract, disclose late.

nodes.label: The 2026 record
nodes.summary: Deleted files, an escape to Hugging Face, real systems reached in evaluations, an outage called user error.

nodes.label: Stated more carefully
nodes.summary: The cases were early rulings, the Air Canada phrase is the tribunal's, the Copilot line is gone; the pattern survives.

nodes.label: Nothing written down
nodes.summary: Between allow and the failure there is reach and a prompt, and no statement of what the agent must not do.

nodes.label: Agent Behaviour Policy
nodes.summary: The mandate written down beside the measured reach, with explicit prohibitions.

nodes.label: Explicit prohibitions
nodes.summary: Do not send, do not start scheduled tasks, do not attack other sites, speak on your own behalf, make no offers.

nodes.label: Still mostly hope
nodes.summary: A written rule kept by the model and enforced by nobody: an expectation, but on the record.

nodes.label: Liability shifts to the platform
nodes.summary: A prohibition the agent breaks turns you allowed it into the product ignored what it was told.

nodes.label: Towards the world, the deployer
nodes.summary: Customers and regulators deal with the deployer; the moment of authorisation is the grant.

nodes.label: Software as a product
nodes.summary: The EU product liability rules apply from 9 December 2026; the Bundestag passed Germany's version on 8 October.

nodes.label: A policy beside every prompt
nodes.summary: Every agent in a loop, anything with the lethal trifecta, takes a behaviour policy as a separate input.

nodes.label: The vendor's half
nodes.summary: Accept the policy, honour it, enforce what the platform can see, report every breach and near miss.

nodes.label: Will vendors accept it?
nodes.summary: Whether platforms will take business rules as an input and answer for them.

quotes.text: The shell game works because nothing was written down.
quotes.why: The diagnosis the post's four moves share.

quotes.text: It is about whether the product did what it was explicitly told.
quotes.why: Where the written policy moves the dispute.

articles.title: Dark mode, and four more: five themes for the newsroom, chosen once and kept in your browser
articles.teaser: Five themes behind one pill in the bar, kept in the reader's browser, built as a layer over a stylesheet this site cannot edit, with colour as a token and a test.

figures.caption: The Industry Wire in the five themes, at 1440 pixels: Newsprint, the look since v0.6.0 and still the default; Night, the dark mode that was asked for; Paper, warm cream with terracotta; Blueprint, white with electric blue; Ember, dark with amber. The same page, the same stylesheet, one attribute on the html element changed.

The picker, open, on the wire in Night. The pill beside Vault shows a swatch and the name of the theme the page is in. The list shows five, each with its own swatch, its name and three words on what it is; the current one is in the accent and bold.

The wire in Night, at 1440 pixels. The teal is lifted two steps from Newsprint's so it holds 4.5:1 on the dark page, and links take the lighter teal, because on this site the "dark" accent is the link colour and dark is the wrong direction on a dark page. The terminal-style status box stays dark in every theme, the way a terminal is.
The bar at 2000 pixels, one row: the brand and the version, eight groups, and the tools as one cluster on the right. Before v0.12.12 this width showed GitHub alone on a second row.
The bar at 1279 pixels, the first width below the limit: the groups are behind Menu and the tools stay on the bar, so the balance, the vault and the theme are one tap.

graph.teaser: Five themes behind one pill in the bar, kept in the reader's browser, built as a layer over a stylesheet this site cannot edit, with colour as a token and a test.
graph.core_idea: A reader's two-word reply became five themes: the look the site had stays the default, pixel for pixel, and four more reach every heading because every colour on the site now comes from one file of tokens, with the imported stylesheet's literal colours shadowed rule by rule rather than edited, the theme set before the first paint, and a test that fails on a theme with a hole or a stylesheet with a literal.

nodes.label: Dark mode!
nodes.summary: The first reaction to the wire from outside: a reader on WhatsApp, two words, which became Dinis's ask for five themes like VoiceDebrief's.

nodes.label: Five themes
nodes.summary: Newsprint, the default and unchanged; Night, the dark mode; Paper, warm cream; Blueprint, white and blue; Ember, dark and amber.

nodes.label: The pill in the bar
nodes.summary: A swatch and a name beside Search and Vault; a list of five with a swatch, a name and three words each; keyboard and touch.

nodes.label: Kept in this browser
nodes.summary: The choice lives in localStorage and never leaves the device; the system's dark preference decides only until the reader chooses.

nodes.label: A stylesheet this site cannot edit
nodes.summary: The newsroom's look is sgit.ai's stylesheet, imported on every sync and checked unedited, and it writes forty-odd colours as literals.

nodes.label: The override map
nodes.summary: Every rule with a literal is restated later in the cascade with a token whose Newsprint value is that literal: same selector, same specificity, generated from a script, not guessed.

nodes.label: Colour is a token
nodes.summary: A stylesheet names a colour through a token, defined once in all five themes; the stylesheets this site owns were rewritten to the rule.

nodes.label: Before the first paint
nodes.summary: The theme stylesheet and a classic, blocking script are the first lines of the body on every page, so a page opens in the reader's theme rather than flipping.

nodes.label: --head, not --ink
nodes.summary: A token is named for what it is for: the imported deck viewer reads --ink as a dark bar, so a near-white heading token under that name would have turned the bar white.

nodes.label: The bar on one row
nodes.summary: Eight groups, the tools as one cluster, the parent pill gone, breakpoints found by a sweep of widths and kept by the test.

nodes.label: The test
nodes.summary: Every token in every theme; no literal outside the themes file; the picker and its memory; contrast at 4.5:1 measured in every theme; the bar on one row from 1200 up.

nodes.label: White on white
nodes.summary: The map's .btn rule outranked the wire's own button and the first screenshot showed an empty pill; the fix is specificity, and the lesson is in the guidance.

nodes.label: The design guidance
nodes.summary: assets/themes/README.md: the tokens and what each is for, what stays literal and why, and how to add a theme.

quotes.text: Newsprint renders pixel for pixel as before, and the other four reach every heading.
quotes.why: The whole design constraint and its answer in one sentence.

quotes.text: A token is named for what it is for, not for what it looks like in one theme.
quotes.why: The naming rule, learnt from a bar that would have turned white.

articles.title: The vault crosses Chrome profiles: state and memory between browser sessions, found by using it rather than by building it
articles.teaser: The reader's vault carries the newsroom between Chrome profiles as it does between devices, a way to share state across browser sessions nobody built.

figures.caption: Two Chrome profiles on one computer, each signed in to a different Google account, each with its own local storage that the other cannot see. The reader's vault sits outside both: each profile writes its own file to it and reads the other's, so the marks, the reading and the balance in one are there in the other. The way in differs by where the passkey lives.

Six steps, three days, and not a straight line. Each of the first five was built for its own reason, following what the reader valued; the sixth was not built at all, it was found by using the others. Dates and releases from the release histories of sgit.ai and the newsroom.

graph.teaser: The reader's vault carries the newsroom between Chrome profiles as it does between devices, a way to share state across browser sessions nobody built.
graph.core_idea: Because the reader's state is records in a vault, one file per device, a second Chrome profile is just another device, so the vault gives a person memory and state between browser sessions and accounts, the way sgit already does for agents, and it was found by using the newsroom rather than built.

nodes.label: Separate Chrome profiles
nodes.summary: Each Google account in its own profile, with its own history, passwords, cookies and site storage.

nodes.label: Moving state between them

nodes.label: Activity in local storage
nodes.summary: The reading meter recorded reads, spend, personas and ratings in the browser on 10 October.

nodes.label: I miss it
nodes.summary: Four devices, four balances: the value to the reader made the activity worth keeping.

nodes.label: The reader's vault
nodes.summary: Three sgit vaults opened from a passkey in the browser, one file per device, the view computed.

nodes.label: Marks and a stake
nodes.summary: Notes like read later and not for me, and seen wire stories, gave the reader a reason to keep their newsroom.

nodes.label: Across devices
nodes.summary: The feature asked for: every device's activity in the browser you hold, one balance.

nodes.label: Across profiles
nodes.summary: The feature found: a second profile is a second device to the vault, so the state crosses.

nodes.label: A door per way in

nodes.label: Profiles are more common
