articles.title: Firing journalists is the worst thing a publication can do: what a hiring decision says about where a publisher is going, and who to hire instead
articles.teaser: A hiring decision is a direction of travel: fire the journalists and the centre of gravity moves to packaging, where the metric makes clickbait by construction.

figures.caption: A cut says the centre of gravity is moving to packaging; a hire says it is staying on the content and getting tooled; and five counts let anyone read which from outside. Below, the two failure modes and the case this site makes.

graph.teaser: A hiring decision is a direction of travel: fire the journalists and the centre of gravity moves to packaging, where the metric makes clickbait by construction.
graph.core_idea: Against the 2026 job-cut figures, a publisher's hiring decisions are read as the clearest statement of where its centre of gravity is going: firing the people who make original content and hiring for traffic moves the centre to packaging, where measuring engagement makes clickbait by construction because what you measure is what you become; firing the engineers fails the other way, with journalism nothing enables; the case is to keep and tool the journalists, hire the roles that turn a notebook into a graph and the engineers who build what the tooling needs, measure value to the reader, and read any publisher's real strategy from outside with five counts.

nodes.label: The 2026 cuts
nodes.summary: Press Gazette's tracker: 3,434 in 2025, 3,875 in 2024, about 6,000 in 2023; in 2026 the BBC, the Washington Post, Reach, Scripps and McClatchy, with the Idaho Statesman losing 10 of 18 reporters.

nodes.label: A hiring decision is a direction of travel
nodes.summary: The clearest statement a publisher makes about where its centre of gravity is going, because it is what the company actually spent.

nodes.label: The centre of gravity
nodes.summary: Where the thing the organisation exists to make is made, and where the power is; in a news publisher, the journalists.

nodes.label: What you measure is what you become
nodes.summary: Hire for engagement and the metric becomes pages opened; optimise for it and clickbait follows by construction; the metric is a hiring plan in disguise.

nodes.label: Failure mode: all packaging
nodes.summary: A coherent business whose world is shrinking: referrals down 58%, newsrooms down 57%, answer engines fetching thousands of pages to send back ten readers.

nodes.label: Failure mode: no engineers
nodes.summary: Journalism that nothing enables: no graph, no checkable provenance, no versions, no surfaces for agents, no meter.

nodes.label: Who to hire instead
nodes.summary: Keep and tool the journalists; hire historians, cartographers, ontologists and librarians, AI-enabled; hire the engineers and AI product managers; measure value to the reader.

nodes.label: Five counts from outside
nodes.summary: Original share, sourcing, corrections, roles hired against roles cut, and the metric the publisher itself reports.

nodes.label: We hire the ones you let go
nodes.summary: Unsourced: the good ones leave first because they want to do the work; in publishing they are the journalists.

nodes.label: This makes you better, not this replaces you
nodes.summary: The tooling handed to journalists as an advantage is the business case of most of this site.

quotes.text: The metric is a hiring plan in disguise.
quotes.why: The sentence for a board.

quotes.text: Fire the journalists and there is nothing to capture. Fire the engineers and it is not captured.
quotes.why: The two failure modes in one line.

quotes.text: The reporting is done, and then it is thrown away as a PDF of the paper.
quotes.why: What no engineering looks like.

articles.title: The site is an inbox: deciding before reading, marks that build the reader's own graph, and why I could not write this brief until the vault existed
articles.teaser: The site as an inbox that starts empty: decide fast before reading, mark slowly while reading, build a graph you own, and sign what you send to the newsroom.

figures.caption: Two modes. The inbox mode decides what happens to a piece with nothing loaded; the reading mode is where the marks and the signals live. Everything stays in the reader's browser and vault, and the reader chooses what an agent sees.
The reader's graph is made of marks, each with a kind; the marks land on the public graphs this site already publishes; a chosen slice goes to the newsroom, signed; a new version comes back.

graph.teaser: The site as an inbox that starts empty: decide fast before reading, mark slowly while reading, build a graph you own, and sign what you send to the newsroom.
graph.core_idea: With the reader's vault live, the next brief treats the site as an inbox that starts empty: every piece, original or aggregated, waits for a one-tap decision in a fast inbox mode with nothing loaded, and only reading is the slow mode, where marks of six kinds become nodes in a graph the reader owns, connected to the graphs the site publishes for every article; scroll depth, awake time and from-and-to are recorded for the reader and kept as the meter keeps everything, in the browser and the vault; personas each have a key pair so a comment to the newsroom goes down the write-only lane signed with a copy kept; nothing is gamified; and the brief could only be written once the properties of what runs became the constraints to think with.

nodes.label: The constraints are what let me think
nodes.summary: The brief could not be written until the vault ran; five properties of what runs closed the design space enough to think in a morning.

nodes.label: The site is an inbox
nodes.summary: It starts empty; every piece, original or aggregated, waits for a decision; deciding is the work and reading is one of the decisions.

nodes.label: The inbox mode
nodes.summary: With nothing loaded, one tap: read now, read later, not for me, more like this, less like this, comment, move to a persona.

nodes.label: The reading mode
nodes.summary: The piece open, the pane about it: its graph, the reader's marks, the decisions, the cost.

nodes.label: No gamification
nodes.summary: A decision is offered where the reader would take it, never at the end of a page; a signal the site engineered is not a signal.

nodes.label: Marks of six kinds
nodes.summary: Interesting, great phrase, not sure, fact, evidence, question: each a node with the phrase, the article, the version, the persona and the time.

nodes.label: The reader's own graph
nodes.summary: Marks connect to the public article graphs; meaning comes from connectivity; the graph is worth more the more it is used.

nodes.label: The free signals
nodes.summary: Scroll depth as read or glanced, time while awake, from and to, the decisions; kept in the browser and the vault, seen by an agent only through a read key.

nodes.label: Personas with keys
nodes.summary: Disposable, one key pair each; the editor persona comments on everything; a persona can be handed to an agent as a read key to its slice.

nodes.label: The signed lane
nodes.summary: A mark for the newsroom is encrypted to its published key, signed by the persona, copied to the vault; the reply is a new version.

nodes.label: The bet
nodes.summary: The loop closes only if reading with a graph that grows is better than reading without one.

nodes.label: What to build, in order
nodes.summary: Inbox mode on the wire first, the pane about the piece, marks, signals, persona keys, the signed lane, the views, an experiment per feature.

quotes.text: Deciding is the work; reading is one of the decisions.
quotes.why: The inbox in one line.

quotes.text: Ship first, think second, and do not pretend the thinking could have come first.
quotes.why: The order the feedback loop runs in.

quotes.text: I am not highlighting any more. I am building my graph.
quotes.why: What kinds of mark change.

articles.title: The vault is live: from a design on 11 October to a reader's vault on newsroom.sgit.ai by two in the morning, and how all of it fits together
articles.teaser: The reader's vault runs on newsroom.sgit.ai: a passkey opens three real vaults, each device writes one file, and the architecture is drawn as it stands.

figures.caption: What is running on newsroom.sgit.ai at v0.11.0: the meter and local storage as before; the vault pane and one module over the vendored vault library, new; the vault server holding ciphertext. On the right, the three vaults, what each holds, and how one gesture opens all three.

The pane, on an article, before it is enabled: the device's id, a label for it, the two ways in, one paragraph that says what the passkey does, and the list where every call to the vault server will appear.

Cards 3 and 4 of the passkey lab: the derivation from the bytes to the door, timed on the device, and the recovery code that derives a second door. Card 6, where the account was first built as three real vaults, appears on a browser with a platform authenticator; this headless one has none.

Two devices, one passkey, one view. Each device writes its own file, whole, when its reader presses Update; the vault holds records, never totals; opening the vault computes one view from every file; brought-in records keep their author.
The page that explains the vault and opens the pane on arrival: the loop in five steps, the principles, what leaves the browser, and a block for an agent.

graph.teaser: The reader's vault runs on newsroom.sgit.ai: a passkey opens three real vaults, each device writes one file, and the architecture is drawn as it stands.
graph.core_idea: Between the morning of 11 October and 02:22 UTC on 12 October the reader's vault went from a design to a running feature on newsroom.sgit.ai: a Vault pane on every page enables the account with a passkey, creates a door at its derived address, a master and a reader vault as real sgit vaults through the vendored vault library, writes each device's raw records as one file in one commit, and brings other devices' activity into the browser so the meter shows one balance; local storage stays primary, the vault holds records never totals, one file per device means no conflict by construction, eight test files run in CI against a mock of the vault server plus a CLI round trip, and a live check on an iPad confirmed it; the properties of what runs are the constraints the next brief is thought with.

nodes.label: Not built

articles.title: Two agents, one vault: the Industry Wire is written into an encrypted vault by one agent and drawn by newsroom.sgit.ai, which holds only the read key
articles.teaser: One agent writes the Industry Wire into an encrypted vault; newsroom.sgit.ai holds only the read key and draws it, so a commit reaches the page with no release.

figures.caption: Two agents, one vault. The wire desk writes the vault with a key the site never holds; the vault server holds ciphertext; newsroom.sgit.ai holds the read key and draws what the reader's browser decrypts. The timeline is from the two git logs.

The wire's edition page on 12 October. The grey line is the vault's own head: its id, the time the pointer was checked, the commit and its message. Then the editor's note and the three threads of the week, read from the vault seconds earlier.

The lead story as the page draws it: date, publisher, source kind, confidence, why it leads, the summary, the quote with its source, why it matters, who else covered it, the entities, and the status the vault gave it.

Under the Dinis lens, two stories in the first beat are withheld, and the page says why: no concern matched, and the ten concerns that were tried. The next beat says five reach and three are withheld.
The personal brief under the Dinis lens: the note, seven stories by score with the concerns that matched, and the sentence that says why a brief for one person is on a public page.
The vault opened as its own app, read-only, with the public key: the same edition, the same lens, the same numbers, drawn by the code inside the vault rather than by the newsroom.
How the wire works, on the newsroom: how the site reads the vault, the contract between the vault and the site, and the clone command with the read key, which is the whole credential.

graph.teaser: One agent writes the Industry Wire into an encrypted vault; newsroom.sgit.ai holds only the read key and draws it, so a commit reaches the page with no release.
graph.core_idea: A vault is the right interface between two agents that never share a session: the wire desk writes 40 stories, 55 sources, 7 personas and a code-only join into an encrypted sgit vault with a write key the site never holds; newsroom.sgit.ai holds the published read key and about four hundred lines that open the vault in the reader's browser, decrypt it and draw it as text, with 28 checks against the real vault in CI; the site owns the presentation and the vault owns the news, a commit is on the page within two minutes with no release, the server sees ciphertext, the history is the audit trail, and the site's agent read the whole vault before publishing the key and held back the one named reader's lens until that person agreed in writing.

nodes.summary: A week of industry news across five beats, read live from a vault on newsroom.sgit.ai, with a lens per persona and one named reader.

nodes.label: Vault u9i9jp0l

nodes.label: The join is code, not a model

articles.title: The article remains a product: Jonathan Palmer's four outputs for a newsroom with no human readers, checked against one that runs
articles.teaser: Jonathan Palmer's four outputs for a newsroom with no human readers, quoted line by line and checked against newsroom.sgit.ai as it runs, screenshots included.

figures.caption: His four outputs, against what runs. Each row quotes one output from Jonathan Palmer's post; the middle column is the page on newsroom.sgit.ai that does it today, the right-hand column is what is only designed. The line between them is the newsroom's own dated page of what runs.

The articles as graphs, on newsroom.sgit.ai. Every article drawn in date order round the circle, sized by how many others link to it: 74 articles, 349 links between them, and 10 amber links where an older article was updated to point at a newer one. One graph per article follows below the map.

The World News Day graph: 21 op-eds as 160 nodes and 427 edges, with the three machine surfaces linked at the top. The box under it is the rule the section is built under: hold the pieces, republish none, and fail the build if twelve consecutive words of any piece appear.

A live article with its five readers folded under the abstract: two minutes, the arc, nine slides, a map, and 137 catalogued items, six of them flagged. The views are extracted from the article and do not change its version.

The version page of One article, five readers: v1.0.0 on 10 October, v1.1.0 on 11 October, +11 words, one paragraph changed, each with its commit. The sentence changed was a correction, found by the article that followed it.
What changed, paragraph by paragraph: 63,000 words became 65,000, 122 releases became 123, and a phrase was rewritten. The tool that draws this was built on the same day as the revision.

The published vault: one read key, printed in full, is the whole credential. It opens the World News Day corpus as an app in the reader's browser, read only, no account, nothing to install, and no write capability in it.

Contextual validation, not truth: the value split the design argues for, and the sentence that says what is billable. The page is marked as a design, and the newsroom's ledger says nothing is paid upstream.
The first screen of the newsroom's llms.txt: the honest sentence, where the pages come from, and the surfaces an agent may rely on. The chip at the top of every imported page points here.
The newsroom's own ledger, as of 10 October 2026: what runs, its limits, and below it what is designed and not running. Every claim in this article about what is live was checked against this page.

graph.teaser: Jonathan Palmer's four outputs for a newsroom with no human readers, quoted line by line and checked against newsroom.sgit.ai as it runs, screenshots included.

figures.caption: What stays and what moves, measured on newsroom v0.8.0. The publication stays where it is; everything the reader does, the meter, the payments, the personas, the lists, the sharing, moves to a repository of its own, with its own engineering.
Six phases, from mapping to the explorer's return. Until phase five, no behaviour changes, not a feature and not a fix.
Every commit, merge, release and night, with what runs at each and the time it should take. Slow checks run at night, not on the commit.

To keep shipping fast without breaking anything, the reader application moves to its own repository, which both sites consume, as a pure refactoring, proved by the live site serving the same bytes, then goes through the explorer-to-villager phases: map, test with bugs as passing tests and no mocks, review with every finding a GitHub issue, refactor until no adversarial change slips through, and only then new features. A pipeline under two minutes per commit runs Node and three browser engines, with pre-production on a Stripe test link, synthetic readers and a live check at release.

articles.title: The passkey opens the vault: a door per path, a master vault for every user, and no server of ours
articles.teaser: Tested: a passkey's PRF bytes compute a door that holds the master's key, and a different path to the same passkey gives different bytes, so a door per path.

figures.caption: The key chain, after the test. The passkey's PRF output, by one path, computes a door; the door holds the master vault's key and a record of where it came from; the master holds the keys of everything else and the list of its doors. A different path to the same passkey can give different bytes, and gets a door of its own.
The places the key could live, and how you would find each before you could open it. Deriving the door from the passkey needs nothing to be found; the stored options become backups.

The first device, a new device on a path that has a door, adding a door while unlocked, a new device on a path with no door yet, and a lost device. Every step runs in the browser, against the passkey store for the gesture and the vault server for ciphertext.

Where a passkey can live, what each place needs, whether the passkey travels, whether it can return the PRF bytes, and what that means for the reader. The ladder below the table is what the page offers when PRF is off.

graph.teaser: Tested: a passkey's PRF bytes compute a door that holds the master's key, and a different path to the same passkey gives different bytes, so a door per path.
graph.core_idea: An end-to-end, client-side account with no sign-in to the site: a passkey with the WebAuthn PRF extension gives 32 bytes only the user's authenticator can produce for the site, and because sgit vault keys are made in the client the browser computes a door vault's key and address from them, so nothing is stored or found first; the door holds the master vault's key and a record of its provider, path, credential id, device and date, and the master holds the keys of the vaults below, received read keys, the access key, key pairs generated at random and never derived from the passkey, and the list of its doors. A test on newsroom.sgit.ai on 11 and 12 October 2026 held for the platform path, the derivation and a door on a real server, and showed that the same passkey reached by a phone over QR gives different bytes, so the claim is narrowed to the same kind of path and the unit of the design is a door per path: added in the first week while unlocked with no key typed, bootstrapped by the recovery code where no device has both paths, with an unknown address meaning no door here yet and a door retired by deleting its file, never by destroying its derived address.

Use it, miss it, write the brief, ship it, and use it again. This week the loop ran three times; the fourth turn is this article.

articles.teaser: The people I advise read through agents. Content needs a second package, a brief for their agent, and memory, so it reads what changed, not everything.

figures.caption: The routes a message takes now. Me to the person, and increasingly me to the agent that works for them, which checks what I wrote and explains what applies. My agent to their agent is next.

Start from scratch, or continue from the delta. Without memory, every visit reads everything again. With it, the agent keeps what it read and asks only for what changed. The two numbers are measured; the delta is the design.

A pack for Steve's agent, from Dinis: the same reading list as the link, as plain text, with the reasons, the markdown copy and graph of each article, rules for reading critically, and where to continue. The numbers are real; the changes file is proposed.

graph.teaser: The people I advise read through agents. Content needs a second package, a brief for their agent, and memory, so it reads what changed, not everything.
graph.core_idea: Readers increasingly read through an agent. A founder gave an article on threat tiers to their agent, which saw the team defending against states while backups were undone and reset the target to T3. So content should travel by several routes: to the person, to their agent as a plain-text brief with the articles by number, reasons, graph slices and rules for critical reading, back from the agent to the person as a translation, and later agent to agent through an encrypted lane. Articles are compression we control, which keeps workflows affordable; an agent with an account and memory should read only the delta, which is what it would pay for. Packs must be written safely: data not instructions, nothing hidden, nothing that acts for us, disagreement invited.

The link, part by part. Everything after the # stays in the browser. The article numbers are the contract; the names are display text; nothing in the link should be private, because the link travels in an email.

One feature, five parts of a company, and the loop that connects them. Each hand-off is a written brief, each part tests what it receives, and the feedback comes back the same way. The four dates are from this week.

articles.title: No server, by design: first I retired the database, now I am retiring the back end
articles.teaser: First the database went, now the back end: the SGit Newsroom runs all its logic in the browser, on commodity servers that cannot read your data.

figures.caption: The SGit Newsroom's architecture. Every piece of application logic runs in the reader's browser. Everything on the server side is a commodity product that holds no logic of ours, and the one that holds the reader's data cannot read it.

How the pattern evolved: from removing the database, through files as the store of record and engines that read them in the browser, to removing the back end. Each step removed a moving part rather than adding one.

The gaps a client-side design leaves, as SG Meter's security model lists them, and what a server would cost to close each one. Every gap changes a number only the person exploiting it can see. A server would close them, and bring accounts, a database, webhooks and a deployment with it.

Releases of sgit.ai per day, 1 to 11 October 2026, from the git log: 114 in eleven days. With no back end, a release is a set of files; there is no migration, no deployment of a server and nothing to roll back but a commit.

graph.teaser: First the database went, now the back end: the SGit Newsroom runs all its logic in the browser, on commodity servers that cannot read your data.
graph.core_idea: After replacing the database with the file system (LETS), the next step is removing the back end: encrypted vaults make the server blind, so the application moves to the browser, leaving only commodity products on the server side; the security gaps this leaves are written down and accepted because they do not match the threat, and the result scales without its complexity scaling and ships as files.

articles.title: The agent is the reader: why agents will pay for graphs, personas and signed claims, because it is cheaper than not paying
articles.teaser: Agents pay to read the raw web and guess its meaning. A curated graph answers for 90% fewer tokens, so paying the publisher is cheaper than not paying.

figures.caption: What five articles became, in tokens. The full catalogue is nearly three times the size of the articles, because every item carries its sentence. An agent does not load it whole: asking about one concept, it loads a median of 2,579 tokens of anchored graph instead of 25,698 of prose.

The readers check each other. Each pass is a verification of the one before: 12,600 tokens per flag for the Librarian, 7,100 per correction for the Cartographer, 154,000 for the Historian's one systematic catch. The loop is worth running; it is also worth stopping.

Projected from 5 to 100,000 articles. The corpus grows in a straight line. An uncurated index grows with it. A curated index grows more slowly, at a rate fitted on five articles and shown as a band. The cost of a question flattens in the graph and rises, or loses recall, in the prose.

The agent pays not to pay. The fee is a share of the tokens it saves; the publisher's cost is building and maintaining the graph; the price passes through to whoever the agent works for; and a signed claim is a second product, with an expiry date that makes it a subscription.

MXC names files, network addresses and the desktop; ACS names tool calls and their arguments; the business logic and the authority above them are the deployer's, and that is where the Agent Behaviour Policy works.

Eight scenarios, three designs. The plain agent leaves every path open. The behaviour policy names every row but bounds none on its own. On top of MXC and ACS, three rows become operating-system boundaries, four become boundaries once the business's rule is written into ACS or the tool, and one stays inside the mandate, where only a named person can accept it.

figures.caption: His words and ours. Each idea in Satya Nadella's post, paraphrased, beside the word this network has been using for it, and the page where that word is defined and worked through.

How the vocabulary was built, in dated public work. Most of it was written in the three weeks before Nadella's post, on top of risk and identity research going back to 2025. The convergence is the point: two very different starting places, one set of conclusions.

Supply and authority, in RiskMandate's terms. The supply arrives with a grant; the authority is a mandate with an issuer, a scope and a clock. The gap between them is derived, and each row of it has a barrier. Only one kind of barrier is a control.

articles.teaser: Vault key management at sgit-ai v0.20.0: the one secret, where keys are kept, how they travel sealed on append lanes, and what comes next.

figures.caption: Where everything lives. Encryption and decryption happen in the client; the edge, the API and the bucket only ever handle ciphertext and hashes of capability keys.
The vault key, the keys derived from it, and the separate credentials made for one job each. The full table, with the prefixes, is on the vault credentials page.
How a new vault key reaches the registry without entering a chat. The flow is documented, for the agent that has to follow it, on the Send a vault key page.
Append lanes: one POST from anywhere, readable only by the vault's owner. One lane per sender, so one can be revoked without touching the others.
Communication vaults: one per pair or group of agents, and one per job. Each agent holds only the keys for the conversations it is part of.
The four tracks we are working on, and the one we depend on. Statuses as of 10 October 2026.

graph.teaser: Vault key management at sgit-ai v0.20.0: the one secret, where keys are kept, how they travel sealed on append lanes, and what comes next.
graph.core_idea: Vaults are encrypted in the client, so the server never holds a key and the key is the whole question. Today vault keys live in a password manager and in a registry vault run by an isolated session; agents that create vaults seal the key to the registry's public key and send it on a write-only append lane, so it never enters a chat. The weakest step is giving a key to another agent, because agent platforms have no per-session secrets. Append lanes carry keys, logs, observations and messages; small communication vaults keep each key's blast radius small and multiply the keys. Next: password manager integrations, secrets.sgit.ai's passkey-unlocked keyring, PKI, and out-of-band decryption.

articles.teaser: An old iMac, the long tail of old versions that projects are not paid to support, measured from public data, and five ways to pay for it, simulated.

graph.teaser: An old iMac, the long tail of old versions that projects are not paid to support, measured from public data, and five ways to pay for it, simulated.
graph.core_idea: Open source is not free: somebody pays, at least in time. The long tail of old versions and old machines is measurable (6.99% of Homebrew macOS install events in 30 days, 16.66% in a year, are on versions older than the newest three) and projects drop it because it has no revenue stream, while vendors such as Oracle and Red Hat turn the same need into large, high-margin support businesses. Pence payments only work aggregated, because a 20p card fee dominates below about five pounds. Simulated over 10,000 draws for one project at Homebrew's scale, micro-paid supported builds cover the long-tail cost in half the draws at about 1.80 pounds a machine a year with typical conversion but never in nine in ten, donations in about a quarter, and customised builds for companies in 94%: the reliable money is companies paying for a build below their own cost of keeping the tool working, sold as value, not as a donation or a weaker free tier.

Six kinds of independence, and which check has which. The drafter re-reading its own draft has none; the guard as it runs today has four; the guard under managed settings, with sources written by someone else, has all six.
The prompt that loaded the guard: "A mod is code Claude wrote; it runs with your permissions." Enabling hot reloading runs every mod Claude writes in this session, and picks up each later change.

graph.teaser: Two emails went out in my voice despite a written rule. The fix: a hook that makes a second model approve every draft, failing closed.

figures.caption: Today: one symmetric read key that encrypts everything, and a write key that only the server checks. Because the read key is symmetric, whoever can read can also create data that decrypts and looks genuine.

Two key pairs, neither derivable from the other: one for reading, one for writing. The data key is sealed to the read public key, heads are signed with the write private key, and the vault id is derived from the write public key.

An inner envelope, sealed to named people's public keys, inside the vault's own encryption. Only the 16-byte file key crosses to wherever the private key lives, including a remote service that can log, approve or refuse each decryption.

One Apple silicon Mac per customer, one agent desktop at a time, and up to two virtual machines where the work is development. Keys come from the owner, encrypted to each desktop's own key; set-up, code, data and policy come from vaults; every request goes through a proxy and gateway, and every event goes to an audit vault.

The calculator: usage, the meter, and five options a month. Every number except Apple's prices is a labelled assumption, with its arithmetic in the vault.

articles.title: Encrypted memory for agents that run somewhere else: sgit deployment patterns, from a Mac mini to Kubernetes
articles.teaser: Agents in isolated, ephemeral places need memory that outlives them. Five sgit deployment patterns, from a Mac mini to Kubernetes, with ciphertext-only servers.

figures.caption: The agents run in isolated places and often only for one task. Each clones the part of the vault it needs, works, commits and pushes, encrypting before anything leaves. The server is yours, it is one container, and what it stores is ciphertext.

The vault server runs as a container next to the agent containers, and its storage is a folder on the Mac mini. Backing up the memory of every agent is copying one folder, and the copy holds only ciphertext.
The compute is disposable and the memory is not. Each run starts from a scoped, shallow clone of the folder the agent owns and ends with a push, so the next run starts where this one stopped.
The vault server is an ordinary Deployment with a volume and a ClusterIP Service. Agents run as Jobs that clone, work, commit and push, and a NetworkPolicy keeps everything else away from the server.

Everything the agents talk to is inside the VPC: an internal load balancer on a private address, and behind it the vault server, either the container on EC2, Fargate or Kubernetes, or the same app on Lambda attached to the VPC, with S3 behind both. The Mac mini joins over a VPN, and CloudFront can give the owner a stable name and TLS without a public address on the server.
A vault is not tied to the server it was created on. Add a second remote and push to it, and any clone with the vault key can restore either server.

figures.caption: Seven levels of agency for anyone, a person or an agent, asked to make a decision. The weakest of seven dimensions caps the level. Below level 3, accountability belongs to whoever designed the decision point; from level 4, the review improves the system that produced the request.
The seven levels in the vault: what the decider can do at each, what agency it gives, and who is accountable.
Fourteen decision points scored by the same rule, from the label prompt at level 0 to the one email an agent may send at level 6.

The review as a loop: read it as the person who will sign it, question each statement, trace where it came from, classify the gap, fix the source, think better, record the outcome, and promote what is proven.
The EU AI Act's human oversight requirements and the guidance on automated decisions, mapped to the seven dimensions. Read together, they put the floor at level 3.

graph.teaser: A yes or no is not agency: seven dimensions, a seven-level scale for people and agents, and the review as a QA step that fixes the source.
graph.core_idea: Agency for anyone asked to decide, a person or an agent, needs options beyond yes, context in their own terms, the ability to look behind what they are shown, time or tokens, symmetric incentives, escalation and authority over the source; the weakest of these caps the decision on a seven-level scale; below level 3 the decider carries liability rather than agency and accountability belongs to whoever designed the decision point and up their chain; above it the review is a QA step that validates everything upstream and fixes the source, and at the top proven cases become rules that run as code under a behaviour policy, which is also what the EU AI Act's oversight requirements already ask for.

articles.title: Hope or enforcement: one customer service agent, three designs, and who keeps each promise
articles.teaser: One customer service agent built three ways, each with an Agent Behaviour Policy: how much of each policy is hope, and what one run can reach.

figures.caption: One customer service mandate, three designs of the agent, and the share of each design's policy that is hope: a rule in prose that only the model keeps. As the reach of one run shrinks, the policy stops having to forbid things.
Design 1 in the vault: one agent, the mail connector and the database connector, and its policy, with every rule marked by what enforces it. Thirty-seven of thirty-eight are expectations.
Design 2: the same agent behind fourteen business tools. Six rules are now enforced by the harness; sixteen are still expectations, because the tools still take a customer or an order as an argument.

Design 3: a code gateway, an intake and security agent, an orchestrator with a routing table, five specialists, a controller and an analyst. Each has a few tools and a short policy, most of it boundaries.

One hostile email through the three designs: a real customer's mailbox, compromised, asks for every open order to go to a new address and for six past orders to be refunded. Designs 1 and 2 hold only if the model holds. Design 3 bounds it, but the model still decides whether the request is genuine.

The analyst's report for one design: every rule, how often ordinary mail exercised it, how often hostile mail tested it, and whether what held was a boundary or the model. Plus tokens against the budget.
The client's view: eight promises a vendor would make about the agent, and for each design what keeps them. Design 1 keeps none by a boundary, Design 2 one, Design 3 six.

graph.teaser: One customer service agent built three ways, each with an Agent Behaviour Policy: how much of each policy is hope, and what one run can reach.
graph.core_idea: Every design of an agent can have a rule for every behaviour; what differs is who enforces each rule and how much the agent can reach, so refactoring a customer service agent from one model with broad connectors, to a harness of business tools, to a team of narrow agents behind a deterministic identity gateway turns most of its policy from expectations the model keeps into boundaries it cannot reach, shrinks the policy because it no longer has to forbid what is impossible, cuts tokens, and leaves a short map of what still rests on hope and which boundary to build next, read after every run and shown to the client as a record rather than a score.

articles.title: Who are you protecting against? Draw the security line where the attacker is, not above it
articles.teaser: Before deciding how secure to be, name the attacker: a six-tier ladder, an air-gapped Mac mini read against it, and eight startups drawing their line.

figures.caption: Six tiers of attacker, from your own mistakes to elevated threats, with what stops each. Most startups plan for everything up to organised crime for money, and write down what they accept above it.

The vault's comparison: the air-gapped, nothing-installed design against an isolated-not-disconnected one, tier by tier. The air gap stops the bots, which no inbound ports and patches also stop; adds a USB path; and gives up backups, monitoring and tooling that would catch the most likely losses.
The vault's compare view: eight fictional startups against the six tiers, the tiers in scope filled and each ceiling marked.

One scenario in full: the accounting firm assistant's assets, its attack tree with an ATT&CK technique on every branch, and the line, with what must be done, what should, what is over the line and why, and the under-engineering to avoid.

The questionnaire: five questions about what you hold, who would pay to attack you, who you sell to, how far one breach reaches and what your customers use today, and the ceiling they point to, with the controls for every tier up to it.

graph.teaser: Before deciding how secure to be, name the attacker: a six-tier ladder, an air-gapped Mac mini read against it, and eight startups drawing their line.
graph.core_idea: Security decisions start with who the threat agent is, what the attack vector is and how sophisticated they are; read against a ladder from your own mistakes to elevated threats, grounded in NIST SP 800-30, the NCSC and MITRE ATT&CK, most startups should plan up to organised crime for money, do the basics consistently because they beat most attackers, sell something better than the customer's baseline rather than beyond their needs, prefer isolation and visibility over disconnection, and write down what they accept above their ceiling, because drawing the line too high slows everything, can create new holes and can stop the technology being used.

articles.title: Every mistake added a rule: complexity, agents, and the way back to shipping
articles.teaser: When every agent mistake adds a rule, complexity wins: map the process, move each piece right as a small shipped component, and keep the rigour for the work.

figures.caption: Two ways to answer a mistake an agent makes. Add a rule, and the prompt grows, the session compacts sooner, and compaction decides which rules survive. Ship a component, and the mistake stops being possible, so the rule can go.

Map one: the verification as it runs. The person preparing the install needs confidence the tool is safe, which comes from a report, which rests on the tool's tests, holding, and on a team of agents. The six things that keep failing sit in a blob on the left, each rebuilt by hand inside a prompt every session. Files, hashes and git sit at the far right, unused.

Map two: the same verification with each piece of process made small and drawn moving right. The tool's tests and the judgment in the report stay custom, because that is the work. Everything else becomes boring on purpose, leaning on files, hashes and git.

How the components compounded on this site, read from the bottom: sgit and encrypted vaults, vault apps and the publishing method, files as the database through Email-FS and Issues-FS, fractal semantic graphs, Agent Behaviour Policies, the agent team, and on top the story vaults and the bridge simulation. Each layer shipped before the next leaned on it.

graph.teaser: When every agent mistake adds a rule, complexity wins: map the process, move each piece right as a small shipped component, and keep the rigour for the work.
graph.core_idea: Founders who now work as engineers with agents often meet complexity not in their code but in the process around it, and answer each mistake with a rule, which grows the prompt, brings compaction sooner and breeds new mistakes; on a Wardley map that complexity is a position, custom-built process sitting where commodities already exist, and the way out is to make each piece a small, tested, shipped component that moves right and no longer needs a rule, with short sessions, memory as versioned files, security matched to assets and attack vectors, rules only for incidents and machines for enforcement, and shipping as the discipline that keeps blast radius and over-engineering under control.

articles.title: The bridge, followed to the end: what one local story is worth when it is kept as a graph
articles.teaser: A bridge closure simulated on a story vault: newsworthy on 5 days, needed on 57, used by three readers, four buyers and an agent, and paid back to its sources.

figures.caption: The Wendmouth Courier on 2 November, in the simulation: the headline is one projection of the story graph, and the tracker beside it shows every source's reopening date. Everything in the simulation is fictional.

Three answers to the only question that mattered, as the newsroom held them on 15 October: an official estimate, a documented contract and an expert assessment, each with its evidence and a confidence that comes from how independent that evidence is.
Top: what each source said the reopening date would be, day by day. Bottom: the five days the paper led with the story, against the fifty-seven days readers needed its current state.
The Courier on the five days the bridge was news, each front page one projection of the story graph with the tracker beside it, and the fifty-seven days in between that readers needed it.
Three readers' graphs meet the story graph at shared anchors: the bridge, the footbridge, the bypass, a bus route and a stop. Green claims are current; grey ones have been superseded and are kept.
Hannah's graph meets the story graph: her home, her children's school, her routines and routes on the left, held on her device; the anchors both graphs share; the claims that reach her through them.
What Hannah received, as WhatsApp messages from the tracker: seven messages over seven weeks, each one about her route, each with its source.

One question an agent asks every morning: is the bridge open, and when will it be? Searching on its own, it reads six pages, spends about sixteen cents and finds the council's first page; asking the newsroom, it spends about two cents and is right.

Who paid, and where it went: £2,707 from 1,596 readers and businesses, three institutions and an agent; 60% to the Courier, which pays the reporter's base salary out of it, a 20% commission to the reporter, 10% to the evidence contributors, 10% to infrastructure and payments. The prices, volumes and split are assumptions written in the vault's build script.
The vault, view by view: twenty of its twenty-three views, in the Day theme, the nine added in version 0.2 outlined.
Revenue against cost, day by day, crossing on 5 November; and the same story with more or fewer followers, where fixed costs stay put and variable costs follow use.
Revenue by month over two years, by who paid: the town in October and November, institutions and agents after that, against a cost that is almost all in the first two months.
Revenue by month across twelve stories: stories in their first three months in blue, the long tail of older stories in orange, which grows with every story added.
The relief scheme without and with the tracker: when the budget was set, who heard about it, who was paid, and what it cost the council to process.
A simulated model query: when will it reopen, asked on 16 October, answered from the three live claims with citations, and the context the model would be given.
The story as an API: every endpoint a GET, every response a file in the vault.
Four themes, one set of tokens: the same view in Night, Day, Paper and Ember.
What the editor expected, and what the town paid for: five of twelve agreed; the town cared more about the bridge than the newsroom did.

articles.title: Story vault underneath, Reader Skills on top: why local journalism has the most to gain

articles.title: Zoom into an agent's behaviour policy and you find the business logic
articles.teaser: Below the first rules, an agent's behaviour policy is the business: functions, processes, clients, values. Layered, owned, counted, and where vendors plug in.

figures.caption: One fictional firm's email agent, layer by layer, with the barrier that stands in the way of each rule. The bottom two layers are mechanics; the four above them are the firm's business.
The worked example, counted. Each rule is backed by a control, governed by an accepted risk with an owner and an expiry, or resting on hope. The proportions are illustrative; the shape is the point.
Five rules from the example, and the control that would move each one. Every control is a kind of product that already exists; what is new is that it enforces a rule the customer wrote.

graph.teaser: Below the first rules, an agent's behaviour policy is the business: functions, processes, clients, values. Layered, owned, counted, and where vendors plug in.
graph.core_idea: The first rules written for an agent are mechanical and vendors enforce them well, but every layer above them is the company's own business logic: how a function is done, the steps a process goes through, who a client is right now, and what the company is for; much of that logic was never written down because software enforced it by omission, and agents working through APIs bypass that; a behaviour policy built in layers, each refining the one below with its own owner, can hold it, can count how much of it is backed by a control, by an accepted risk or by hope, and gives vendors a written rule to enforce and a number to move, which is what lets the business hand work to agents and scale.

nodes.label: The bottom layers are mechanics
nodes.summary: Own account, secrets held by the platform, tools switched off, sending needs a person: boundaries vendors enforce well.

nodes.label: send_message ran with no prompt
nodes.summary: The measured Gmail deployment: thirty tools, sending unprompted, trashing behind an approval. Mechanics need measuring.

nodes.label: Above the mechanics is the business
nodes.summary: Function, process, relationship and organisation layers, each a set of rules a manager would say out loud, each with its own owner.

nodes.label: Vendors cannot model each customer's business
nodes.summary: To scale they build what is the same for everybody; the business layers differ per company and are often unwritten.

nodes.label: Software was the law
nodes.summary: Approval chains, RBAC and workflows encoded the rules; a missing button was a control.

nodes.label: Agents work through the API, not the screen
nodes.summary: The rule the interface enforced by omission is no longer enforced unless it is written down.

nodes.label: Policies inside policies
nodes.summary: Each layer refines the one below inside the room it allows, from tool permissions up to what the company is for.

nodes.label: Shared facts, own formulas, declared bridges
nodes.summary: The ABP vocabulary's three layers: customers extend it in their own vault without changing the shared one.

nodes.label: Control, accepted risk, or hope
nodes.summary: Each rule is backed by a boundary, governed by a named acceptance with an expiry, or resting on hope; the counts are the finding.

nodes.label: Five, six and six of seventeen
nodes.summary: In the fictional firm the platform layer is all control and the organisation layer all hope.

nodes.label: A vendor control moves one written rule
nodes.summary: Send gateways, content checks, ledger approvals and blocked-recipient lists each move a rule from hope or acceptance to control.

nodes.label: Frameworks already ask for the description
nodes.summary: AI BCF RG.2 asks that what an autonomous system does is described; AC.3 asks for a named owner.

nodes.label: The upper layers read like skills
nodes.summary: A skill says how; a policy layer says what is allowed, who owns it and what stands in the way. Together they codify the business.

nodes.label: A real inbox, layered and counted
nodes.summary: Write the upper layers above the measured Gmail deployment, publish the counts, then again with a vendor's control in the path.

quotes.text: The rule that the user interface enforced by omission is no longer enforced, unless somebody writes it down and something enforces it.
quotes.why: Why agents force business logic out of software and into policy.

quotes.text: A control attached to a written rule is worth more than one switched on in general, because the customer can see what it bought.
quotes.why: Why the behaviour policy is a good integration point for vendors.

articles.title: A locked-down desktop for an agent, by the minute, is still hard to rent
articles.teaser: Nine properties a safe agent desktop needs, nine products against them, the macOS day-long lease, and the startup credits that would pay for testing it.

figures.caption: Nine products against the nine properties of a locked-down agent desktop, from each product's own documentation on 7 October 2026. No row has all nine.
The same 44 hours of work a month, at published prices. Where billing follows the work, it costs a few dollars; where the desktop is a leased Mac, two hours buys a day.
The proposal: one mandate per task, a fresh desktop configured from it, three tracks by operating system, and a vault outside every desktop for anything worth keeping.

graph.teaser: Nine properties a safe agent desktop needs, nine products against them, the macOS day-long lease, and the startup credits that would pay for testing it.

articles.title: An open AI governance framework, and what its licence let us build

The framework and the three it maps to, by what their terms allow. Only AI BCF is under a licence written for adaptation that also keeps adaptations open. A summary of published terms, not legal advice.
The conversion. The CSV is kept byte for byte with its SHA-256; one deterministic script builds every other file from it; the AI Act citations are joined to the law's text in another vault.

Five altitudes of the same graph, captured from the vault's graph view: the framework, a category, a control, a cited clause, and the paragraph of the AI Act it resolves to. Each altitude has its own question; the grammar does not change.

SQLite in the browser: which controls cite an article the 2026 amendment changed. Seven rows, in a few milliseconds.
The triple-pattern console: three patterns, joined on shared names, from control to clause to law to the amending act.
A control page: the framework's text verbatim, the "no equivalent" note from its own Sources column, and the overlay set apart and labelled.

graph.teaser: Twenty open AI governance controls under CC BY-SA, why the licence matters, and the same day's conversion into a graph, a database and a walk down to EU law.
graph.core_idea: The AI Baseline Control Framework is a practical, deployer-focused set of twenty AI governance controls in five categories and three types, each with a why and a how and a mapping to the NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001 and the EU AI Act; its Access category covers what an AI system can reach, which the three it maps to do not; its CC BY-SA licence and CSV export let it be converted on the day into a semantic graph with an ontology, a taxonomy, linked data, documents and a browser database, joined by id to a graph of the AI Act, and walked as a fractal graph from the framework down to a paragraph of law, which surfaced findings the list does not state and kept every addition labelled apart from the source.

articles.title: Where is the why? A permission prompt asked me to decide, and kept the reason
articles.teaser: A prompt asked for a decision and kept the reason. Read through the policy, the law on uninformed consent, and the fixes that worked: put the why in the prompt.

figures.caption: What the prompt carried and what it did not: three fields and two buttons on the left; on the right, the six things the person needed to judge the request, none of which were on the screen. Infographic from a screenshot of 7 October 2026.
The prompt as it appeared on 7 October 2026: "Claude wants to add a repository to this session", with the owner, the repository, the access level, and two buttons. Screenshot, cropped.
Decline breaks the work; Allow buys accountability without information; the third answer, a reason, was not offered. From the voice note of 7 October 2026.

The request through the Agent Behaviour Policy's words: the grant before and after, the mandate, the gap, the barrier, the blast radius and the kind of decision, for read access and for write access to the same public repository.
Who carries a decision taken without the information: courts, regulators and research from 1956 to 2023, grouped by where they put the burden. Not legal advice; sources in the Sources section.

Prompts that asked without a why, and the fixes that worked: purpose strings, number matching and context, refusal as easy as acceptance; and the ones still open, from OAuth scopes to agent prompts. Sources and dates in the article.

A proposal: the same request as a why card, with the session and step, the reason quoting the instruction, the change in reach, the cost, the path if declined, the scope and the record; buttons to allow for the task, decline and continue, ask a question, or park it. The reason shown is illustrative.

graph.teaser: A prompt asked for a decision and kept the reason. Read through the policy, the law on uninformed consent, and the fixes that worked: put the why in the prompt.
graph.core_idea: A permission prompt that asks a person to approve an agent's grant change without saying which session asks, why, what changes, what it could cost and what a no would do, leaves the person a choice between breaking the work and owning a decision they could not judge; read through the Agent Behaviour Policy it is a mid-session grant change whose barrier is a human judgement as strong as the information given, and whose risk lies in the combination with what the session already holds; courts and regulators across medicine, contract, data protection and automated decisions mostly put the duty to disclose on whoever asks and deny weight to token sign-offs, while in practice blame lands on the nearest person; the fixes that worked, purpose strings, number matching and context, refusal as easy as acceptance, all put the reason or the context into the prompt; so the proposal is a why card that carries the reason, the change in reach, the cost, the decline path and a record, and becomes a risk acceptance when the risk rises.

nodes.label: Three fields, two buttons, no reason
nodes.summary: Owner, repository, access; Decline or Allow once; not which session, which step, which instruction, what changes or what a no costs.

nodes.label: Decline breaks the work, Allow buys accountability
nodes.summary: Both offered answers carry an unstated cost; the answer that removes both, a reason, was not on the screen.

nodes.label: A prompt is a grant change mid-session
nodes.summary: The question is what the session becomes once it holds this and what it already holds, not whether the resource is safe.

nodes.label: Read is small, write is a publishing channel
nodes.summary: Read of a public repository adds little; write to it from a session holding confidential data adds an exfiltration path.

nodes.label: A barrier that is a person
nodes.summary: Enforced by the host, so the agent cannot click it; as strong as the information the person is given.

nodes.label: 93% approved, 13.6% caught
nodes.summary: Vendor figures: most agent prompts are approved, and planted dangerous commands are rarely caught, less so as prompts pile up.

nodes.label: Fewer prompts leaves the hard ones
nodes.summary: Sandboxing and classifiers remove the easy prompts; the remaining ones need the reason most, and the classifier's own misses are about consent covering the action.

nodes.label: The asker must disclose
nodes.summary: Montgomery, the red hand rule, Berman and Nguyen, the Consumer Rights Act and GDPR Article 7 put the duty to make information usable on whoever asks.

nodes.label: A token sign-off is not a human decision
nodes.summary: WP251 and SCHUFA: oversight must be meaningful, and a determining machine output stays automated even when a person signs.

nodes.label: Blame lands on the nearest person
nodes.summary: Elish's moral crumple zone and the Post Office Horizon cases: in practice the click is the record, and it carries the person's name.

nodes.label: The fixes put the why into the prompt
nodes.summary: Apple's required purpose strings, Microsoft's number matching with app and location, the CNIL's refusal as easy as acceptance.

nodes.label: The why card
nodes.summary: Who asks, why with the instruction quoted, what changes, what it could cost, if you decline, scope and record; allow for task, decline and continue, ask, park.

nodes.label: When the risk rises, a risk acceptance
nodes.summary: A grant change that raises the session's blast radius names who accepts it, for how long and what ends it, and is recorded as such.

nodes.label: Which session asked, and why
nodes.summary: Not known: the prompt did not say; nor whether its fields are configurable; vendor figures not replicated; not legal advice.

quotes.text: A boundary whose enforcement is a human judgement is exactly as strong as the information that human is given.
quotes.why: Why the prompt is a real barrier and a weak one at the same time.

quotes.text: In practice, the click is the record, and the click has the person's name on it.
quotes.why: The gap between where the law puts the duty and where the blame lands.

articles.title: The Mandate Stack: a multi-agent system in production, layer by layer
articles.teaser: A multi-agent system that runs a business every few hours: eight layers, one written mandate per agent, everything a graph, one human who sends.

figures.caption: The Mandate Stack as it runs on 6 October 2026, read from the bottom: compute and channels rented from vendors, then the team's own files, graphs, schedule and policies, then one person above a line of their own. The right column says what each layer gives the team. Infographic from the CRM agent's briefing; everything shown is in use.

Left to right: the outside world writes in by email, by the subscribe form, through other teams' agents and an event extension; the input passes through the layers as data; the person enters from the right through Claude and Gmail, and is the only exit. From the briefing of 6 October 2026; fictional senders.

One Workspace identity, cut into roles. The reader of raw inbound mail has the least power; the roles with more power never read raw mail; the send row has no agent in it. From the briefing of 6 October 2026; agents named by role.

One person's subgraph in the relationships vault, with a fictional person, organisation and interests. An interest met by one of the team's materials is a reason to send it; an interest with no edge is a gap. Contexts are further graphs laid over the same people. The folder behind the picture is in the lower panel.

One conductor run: open and lock, security, drafts, inbox, briefs, CRM, the event mission, research, dev, security again, a card to Dinis, stop. The order is a design decision. Beside the schedule: emailing the agent, live sessions, joining in two messages. Order from the briefing of 6 October 2026.

Read, eval, print, loop, applied to a business: a friction, a request in the session, a tool as HTML, deployed into the vault, used and corrected. The loop stops when a piece of work no longer calls for a tool. Below: apps already deployed into vaults on this site.

Nine steps, six of them the agents' on the schedule: capture, graph, research, write, register, format. The draft in Gmail is the release candidate. The send is the person's. The recipient's reply comes back through step one. Below: the three causes a mistake is traced to, and the two levels of error correction. From the briefing of 6 October 2026.

What they do not see, the vaults, the sessions, Workspace and encrypted storage, is product or commodity. Rendered with Mermaid wardley-beta from the source below; every placement is a claim.

Map two, from the inside. The anchor is Dinis. articles.title: Why my agents do not run on my laptop: chat, Cowork and Code in the cloud, a vault as the shared drive, and the two walls an operating system has
articles.teaser: An OS has two hard walls, the kernel and the user; an agent on a laptop runs inside the one marked you, so the agents run in the cloud with a vault as shared drive.

figures.caption: Four places the agents run, none of them my laptop, and the one vault they all share. Each surface gets the reach its job needs. The laptop holds the main account and is where I type, not where anything runs. As configured on 6 October 2026.

An operating system has two hard walls, the kernel and the user. An agent on your laptop runs inside the wall marked "you", where everything your account can read is readable. The desktop agents add settings on top. The caveat is in the black bar.

Fifteen months of agents reaching what they were given, July 2025 to September 2026. Every flaw was fixed, most within days; the cloud versions of the same tools were often unaffected. The last column is the point.

The vault as the shared drive between agents. A session is handed a key out of band, pulls, works, commits and pushes; the next session on another surface pulls. The host holds ciphertext. Keys masked, paths illustrative.

The same modest mandate deployed on my laptop and in a cloud session, read as a behaviour policy. On the laptop the grant is the account and most barriers are expectations. In the cloud the grant is built small and most barriers are boundaries. The last row, an instruction hidden in a file the agent reads, has no barrier in either; what differs is what it can reach.

Three things that would change the security of the whole setup and that no platform I use provides yet: an identity per agent, secrets per agent, and a key pair per agent. Each exists in pieces on this site; none is a product feature.

graph.teaser: An OS has two hard walls, the kernel and the user; an agent on a laptop runs inside the one marked you, so the agents run in the cloud with a vault as shared drive.
graph.core_idea: No model runs on the author's laptop because a process there runs as the author and the operating system has no boundary inside a user account between an agent and the SSH keys, cloud credentials, password manager session, browser cookies and files; the desktop agents' prompts and sandboxes are settings enforced by the process they constrain, and fifteen months of incidents show what a mistake or an injected instruction reaches; so the agents run on four cloud surfaces chosen by reach, Claude chat with nothing connected, Cowork with no repositories, Claude Code with one repository and an allowlist, ChatGPT with no assets, and a vault the host cannot read is the shared drive between them, with keys handed per session; the trade-offs are accepted, three wishes remain, identity, secrets and a key pair per agent, and the caveat is that a dedicated machine with separate accounts is a different model to be reported on later.

nodes.label: Why not run it on the laptop
nodes.summary: No business need for an offline model; the one thing a local agent would need to offer, isolation better than the cloud's, is the thing none offers.

nodes.label: An operating system has two hard walls
nodes.summary: The kernel and the user account; inside one account there is no boundary between an agent and the keys, credentials, sessions and files the account can read.

nodes.label: The desktop agents add settings, not boundaries
nodes.summary: Approval prompts, allow lists and process sandboxes are enforced by the process they constrain; the vendor's own docs list credential files as the default read scope and call the boundary a permission prompt.

nodes.label: Fifteen months of incidents
nodes.summary: Deleted home directories and drives, repositories executing before the trust prompt, hidden instructions exfiltrating secrets, tens of thousands of exposed self-hosted gateways, a local sandbox escape reaching SSH keys; every one fixed, the pattern remaining.

nodes.label: The lethal trifecta is the laptop's default
nodes.summary: Private data, untrusted content and a way out are all present on a laptop by default: the account, every file read, and the user's network.

nodes.label: Four places the agents run
nodes.summary: Claude chat with nothing connected for thinking; Cowork in the cloud with no repositories for the team; Claude Code on the web with one repository and an allowlist for code; ChatGPT with no assets as a second model.

nodes.label: The vault is the shared drive
nodes.summary: Encrypted on the agent's side, keys handed per session out of band, clone or pull, work, leak check, commit, push; the next session pulls; the laptop passes keys and nothing else.

nodes.label: Same mandate, two deployments
nodes.summary: On the laptop the grant is the account and barriers are expectations; in a cloud session the grant is small and barriers are boundaries; injection is stopped in neither, and what it reaches differs.

nodes.label: What it costs
nodes.summary: No agents without a connection, a key per session by hand, no per-session secrets in Cowork so one vault per scope, chat without cross-chat memory, two products with two flows; accepted.

nodes.label: Identity, secrets and a key pair per agent
nodes.summary: An agent identity the platform knows with signed commits; secrets injected and revocable per agent; a key pair per agent; each exists in pieces on this site and none as a product feature.

nodes.label: The dedicated machine is a different model
nodes.summary: A second machine with separate accounts and nothing of the author's on it has an empty wall marked that user; closer to the cloud model; to be run and reported on later, not before.

nodes.label: What exists and what does not
nodes.summary: The setup runs and the team's twelve-agent version runs; the three wishes, a desktop agent running as a separate user by default, and the dedicated-machine report do not exist yet.

quotes.text: A mistake inside a boundary is a bad afternoon. The same mistake inside "me" is an incident.
quotes.why: Why hallucination is the wrong word for what goes wrong with a local agent.

quotes.text: The barrier that holds is the small grant, not a cleverer filter.
quotes.why: Prompt injection is not prevented by the cloud; what the injected instruction can reach is.

articles.title: The deck I could not download: an author-first home for presentations, as a business plan somebody else can build
articles.teaser: One download offered as a subscription, an author paid nothing, and a design for the service the author would have chosen: vaults, keys, seven roles, 85% to the author.

figures.caption: The screen that started this, as shown to a reader on 6 October 2026, with the deck and its author left out of the crop. One download offered as a subscription; the author of the deck receives nothing from it. The three complaints, and the one that is not: the licence the author signed allows all of it.
Twenty years of one service. The owner changed twice and the terms changed once; the links did not change at all. In Wardley's terms this is inertia, and it is also the opening.

Every author gets a vault the host cannot read. Who may open a deck is decided by which key a device holds: a publishing key for the author, a content key per deck, a read key for what is free, a receipt turned into a ten-minute key for what is paid once, and a revocable grant for what is private. Design sketch; proposal.

Seven roles: storage host, key service, unlock service, payments, identity and provenance, the front, and add-ons. What each does, what each sees, who could run it, and which exist today. Sovereignty by construction: an archive can hold a nation's authors' ciphertext without reading it.

Pay once and download the original. The payments service sees a payment, the enclave sees a receipt, the host sees a read; none sees all three. The ledger line goes into the author's vault, and the month's statement is computed from lines like it.

Serving an author's whole shelf for a month costs less than the incumbent charges one reader for one download. Where a one-off price goes by card, from 50p to the incumbent's subscription for scale: under a pound the rail eats the price. Illustrative figures with list prices as inputs.

A deck page in the mock, after the pay button: the content credential, the hash, read free in the browser, pay once with the split shown, and the ledger line the payment would write. Fictional author and deck.

The author's own view: the September statement with the add-ons' share, the ledger as it is written, the keys and grants with a mock revoke, and what each of the seven services knows about the author. Nothing in the last list can read a slide except the enclave for one request and the author's own device.

graph.teaser: One download offered as a subscription, an author paid nothing, and a design for the service the author would have chosen: vaults, keys, seven roles, 85% to the author.
graph.core_idea: A reader is sold a 30-day trial and a monthly subscription for a single presentation while the deck's author receives nothing, under an uploader agreement that grants a royalty-free, sublicensable licence to monetise and train models on the work; the platform persists through fifteen years of embeds and links, which is inertia; an author can ask today for counts and recipients under the right of access and, in some EU states, for revenues under the copyright transparency duty; and the service the author would have chosen can be built on this site's primitives: every author's decks in a vault the host cannot read, access decided by keys, decryption in the browser, an attested enclave for the one step that needs plaintext, seven separable roles, pay once with 85% to the author on a ledger they can recompute, provenance as the product; the plan is published as a vault with a working mock, with its economics worked and the card-fee floor stated as the hard row.

nodes.label: One download, one subscription decision
nodes.summary: A 30-day trial then £10.99 a month ($11.99 in the US) for a single file, no one-off option unless the author switched a setting on, which was reported as off by default when the paywall arrived in September 2021.

nodes.label: What the author agreed to
nodes.summary: The uploader agreement grants a royalty-free, sublicensable licence to monetise, charge for, advertise against and train models on the work, and does not entitle the author to any payment; the same company forbids users from training on the content.

nodes.label: Three complaints, and the one that is not
nodes.summary: The reader is sold a subscription for one file; the author has no say and no share; the author does not know where the work went. The licence allows all of it, so the complaint is that the service the author would have chosen does not exist.

nodes.label: Why it has not been replaced
nodes.summary: Fifteen years of embeds, backlinks and search ranking; about forty million visits a month, mostly from search; past success breeds inertia, and the authors' links are what the incumbent holds.

nodes.label: What an author can ask for today
nodes.summary: Switch the download setting on; send a right-of-access request for the counts and the recipients, with the EDPB's derived-data guidance and the Court's ruling on naming recipients; in some EU states, the copyright transparency duty on all revenues generated; the UK did not implement it.

nodes.label: The author holds the keys
nodes.summary: Every author's decks in a vault the host cannot read; a publishing key bound to a passkey; a content key per deck; a read key for what is free; a receipt turned into a ten-minute key; a revocable grant; decryption in the browser; an enclave for the one step that needs plaintext.

nodes.label: Seven roles, no single owner
nodes.summary: Storage host, key service, unlock service, payments, identity and provenance, the front, add-ons; no party holds more than one of the content, the keys and the money; each can be provided per country, profession or company.

nodes.label: Read free, pay once, grant and revoke
nodes.summary: A read is a count on the author's ledger; a one-off payment becomes a receipt the enclave turns into a short key; a grant is wrapped to a recipient and revoked by re-keying; a downloaded file is the reader's and the plan says so.

nodes.label: Near-zero marginal cost, and the card-fee floor
nodes.summary: Serving one author's shelf for a month costs less than the incumbent charges one reader for one download; the hard row is 1.5% plus 20p with a 30p minimum, which the plan states and gets under with wallets, batching and an open payments protocol.

nodes.label: 85% to the author, on a ledger they can recompute
nodes.summary: The platform's 15% pays the card fee and lives on top-ups, batching and add-ons at a 70% author share; the statement is reconciled to the author's ledger, never the reverse.

nodes.label: What the service sells is provenance
nodes.summary: This file, with this hash, published by this person, bound to a key in tiers; a conference, an employer, a journalist and a reader each have a cheap question answered.

nodes.label: The plan as a vault with a working mock
nodes.summary: Ten plan documents, the data, the right-of-access letter, a register of ten accepted risks, and an app of web components bundled for the vault host: the shelf, a deck page, the author's view, the roles, the flows, the economics, the rights.

nodes.label: What exists, and what does not
nodes.summary: Vaults, read keys, lanes and browser decryption exist; the deck enclave, grants as a service, the receipt that becomes a key, the migration tool and a sub-five-pence rail for a person do not; step zero is the author's own 69 decks.

quotes.text: A setting lives on a server and changes when the server's owner changes. A key lives with the author and is verified by anyone.
quotes.why: The whole design in two sentences: access by keys, not by settings.

quotes.text: The right the platform reserves for itself it withholds from its users.
quotes.why: The asymmetry in the terms on model training, stated without overstating the licence.

articles.title: The agent team as it runs: one person, twelve agents, encrypted vaults, and a mailbox nobody sends from
articles.teaser: Twelve agents on dedicated accounts, encrypted vaults as the only memory, messages as files, a folder per person, and a mailbox nobody sends from.

figures.caption: The whole stack in one line: a phone, twelve sessions, encrypted vaults, a Drafts folder, and people. Below the line, the four properties that make it safe to copy. Infographic from the team's field notes of 6 October 2026; no live data.

Four separate identities, and the boundaries between them that hold by construction. A session running as one account cannot reach what another holds; a vault key handed to one session does not open another vault. The strongest barriers in the setup cost a few pounds a month each. Fictional detail; no address beyond the agents' published one.

The roster on 6 October 2026, grouped by what each role touches: the mailbox, the memory, the running of the team, the world outside. The last column is the row that does the work, and it is the same word in eleven of twelve rows.

Left: the mailroom convention and a message as a file. Right: the seven steps of a session and the card that ends it. Along the bottom, the four rules that are never negotiated. Fictional paths and counts.

One folder per person, with a sample of the ledger and the six rules that make the folder trustworthy. The summary is generated from the files beneath it, so it cannot drift from them. Fictional person and content.

The five barriers graded, and the six things the policies caught or showed in the first weeks. Reading the table top to bottom: what touches identity and keys is enforced; what touches mail is a prompt, a setting or a hope.

Public, private-ish, personal. The team's vaults are built to hold the first two and refuse the third, and the rules can be scoped per customer or written to protect the person on the other end. The question in the black bar gets its own document.

Every piece of the setup, and the writing on this site that argued for it, in four colours: policy and control, vaults and keys, graphs and memory, record and interfaces. Nothing in the setup has to be taken on trust; each piece has an argument and the argument has a page.

graph.teaser: Twelve agents on dedicated accounts, encrypted vaults as the only memory, messages as files, a folder per person, and a mailbox nobody sends from.
